newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says removing extreme poverty a feasible goal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says removing extreme poverty a feasible goal.

text.p: With 1.3 billion people around the world barely eking out a living, a new U.N. report released on Thursday argues that abject poverty can be wiped out by the year 2020.

The controversial assumption means accelerating economic growth in 100 countries caught in stagnation or economic decline, and implementing national and international policies targeted at the poorest of the poor. And it means reducing AIDS, wars and the depletion of the environmental resources.

"The dramatic record of poverty reduction in the 20th century shows that we should raise out sights, not downsize our vision for human development," says Richard Jolly, coordinator of the 1997 Human Development Report commissioned annually by the U.N. Development Program (UNDP).

His optimism was based on economic growth over the past two decades that has raised the standard of living for 1.5 billion people. More than three-fourths of the world's population can expect to survive to 40 years of age. Adult illiteracy has been cut by nearly half and infant mortality has been cut by nearly three-fifths.

But at the same time nearly a third of the developing world's population, or 1.3 billion people, live on less than $1 a day; more than 800 million people do not have enough to eat, and people in sub-Saharan African nations die 19 years earlier than those in East Asia.
"None of these depressing developments was inevitable," Jolly said. "And all can be reversed if countries take more seriously the commitments already made to give poverty reduction a high priority."

While China, India, Malaysia, Mauritius and South Korea have sharply reduced poverty in two decades, 510 million people in South Asia and 220 million in Africa live well below the poverty line, the report said. And in Latin America poverty affects 110 million people.

In Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, the transition to a market economy showed a marked deterioration with a quarter of the population or 120 million people living in impoverished conditions compared to 4 million in 1988.

The report maintained that economic growth contributes most to poverty reduction when it expands employment, productivity and wages of the poor and when public resources are channeled into health and education.
"Economic growth does contribute to poverty reduction, though it accounts for only about half of it," the report said. "But lack of sustained growth makes it nearly impossible to reduce poverty."
Among the remedies suggested in the report were:

-- Changing structural inequalities in distributing land, credit, housing and social services. Unequal opportunities in education and employment mean that women have fewer choices in freeing themselves and children from the poverty trap.

-- Raising the productivity of small-scale agriculture. The majority of the poor in developing countries depend on agriculture for their livelihoods, which increases employment and food prices. China, Japan and South Korea reduced poverty through smaller farming enterprises.
-- Promoting small businesses or microenterprises now in the informal sector of the economy. Critical ingredients for government are access to credit, savings and improved infrastructures.

-- Growth strategies that focus on labor-intensive activities, such as production of shoes and textiles, similar to those that helped East Asian countries achieve high growth, full employment and higher wages.

-- A crash program of international aid and national resources in basic social services for poor nations. The cost would be $40 billion a year over the next 10 years. The amount needed to close the gap between the income of poor people and the minimum income they need would cost another $40 billion a year.

-- Reducing government debt and managing globalization more carefully such as the urgent need to treat products of developing countries on a par with those of industrialized countries, especially agricultural exports.
